title: One-dimensional local constraints can always be met by a repetitive pattern

fields.label: Label
fields.value: One-dimensional local constraints can always be met by a repetitive pattern

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: In one dimension, any set of local constraints on cell colors that can be satisfied at all can be satisfied by a simple, purely repetitive arrangement, so simple 1D constraints cannot force complex patterns.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: in one dimension it is possible to prove that any local set of constraints that can be satisfied at all can always be satisfied by some simple and purely repetitive arrangement of colors.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 5, “Two Dimensions and Beyond”; section “Systems Based on Constraints” (from p. 210), p. 211. Scope: one-dimensional local constraint systems (one-dimensional subshifts of finite type)

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch05-15: resolvable-now, resolvability 1.00

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: This is a standard finite-graph consequence for one-dimensional shifts of finite type. The stated scope is exact, and a short checkable proof fully resolves it.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Represent the allowed local words as a finite directed graph. Any nonempty bi-infinite path contains a directed cycle, whose repeated labels give a periodic satisfying configuration; one counterexample would refute the claim.

fields.value:

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The statement is the standard fact that a nonempty one-dimensional subshift of finite type contains a periodic point, proved by finding a cycle in a finite de Bruijn graph. That argument covers every finite local constraint in one dimension, and a small team can check it in days. A concrete constraint can also be audited in SageMath by building the same graph.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Form the de Bruijn graph whose edges are locally allowed colorings. A cycle is a purely repetitive solution; a satisfiable one-dimensional constraint whose graph had no cycle would refute the claim, and the standard cycle argument says that case does not occur.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Local means a finite window, which is the reading the surrounding text supports.

The result is existence of one repetitive solution, not uniqueness.

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: For every one-dimensional local constraint system (a set of allowed length-w colour words over k colours) that admits any bi-infinite satisfying arrangement, there is a purely periodic satisfying arrangement, and its period can be taken at most V = k^(w-1).

fields.label: Method
fields.value: analysis.py encodes each constraint system as a bitmask of allowed length-w words. Satisfiability is decided by iterating a reachability vector over the k^(w-1) de Bruijn vertices for 4V + 1 edge steps (existence of a valid word of length 4V + w). Independently, every period word u with |u| <= V is enumerated (sum of k^p over p = 1..V candidates, each stored as the bitmask of its cyclic length-w windows) and u^infinity is accepted iff its window mask is contained in the allowed set. The two indicators are compared for all 138,856 systems (exhaustive for (k,w) = (2,2), (2,3), (2,4), (3,2), (4,2); seeded samples of 2000 and 5000 for (2,5) and (3,3)); minimal periods are tabulated. Run time about 3 s.

fields.label: Pass criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered: across all enumerated or sampled constraint systems, every system that admits a valid word of length 4V + w (the operational test of satisfiability, independent of any cycle argument) also admits a periodic arrangement u^infinity with |u| <= V whose every cyclic window of length w is allowed; and every system with no such long valid word has no periodic arrangement either. Zero violations in both directions.

fields.label: Fail criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered: at least one constraint system admits a valid word of length 4V + w but no periodic arrangement with period <= V (this would refute the claim as stated, since the shortest possible periodic solution is bounded by V); or the two satisfiability indicators disagree in the other direction, which would indicate a broken test.

fields.label: Unit
fields.value: fraction of satisfiable constraint systems that have a periodic solution with period <= k^(w-1)

fields.label: Uncertainty
fields.value: exact for the exhaustive families; the two sampled families are 2000 and 5000 seeded draws

fields.label: Interpretation
fields.value: Wolfram's 'local set of constraints' on a one-dimensional array of coloured cells (p. 210-211: each cell's neighbourhood must be one of a given set of allowed configurations) is a one-dimensional subshift of finite type: a set of allowed words of a fixed window length w over k colours. 'Can be satisfied at all' is read as the existence of a bi-infinite arrangement all of whose windows are allowed; by compactness this is equivalent to the existence of arbitrarily long valid finite words, and operationally it is tested by the existence of a valid word of length 4V + w (any valid word longer than V must revisit a de Bruijn vertex, so this length is far beyond the threshold, and the check is done by a reachability iteration, not a cycle search). 'Simple and purely repetitive arrangement' is read as a periodic configuration, found by brute-force enumeration of all period words u with |u| <= V = k^(w-1) and checking all cyclic windows. All constraint systems are enumerated exhaustively for (k, w) in {(2,2), (2,3), (2,4), (3,2), (4,2)} and sampled with a fixed seed for (2,5) and (3,3).

fields.label: Datasets
fields.value:
All 16 allowed-word sets, 2 colours, window 2 (generated by analysis.py)

All 256 allowed-word sets, 2 colours, window 3 (generated by analysis.py)

All 65536 allowed-word sets, 2 colours, window 4 (generated by analysis.py)

All 512 allowed-word sets, 3 colours, window 2 (generated by analysis.py)

All 65536 allowed-word sets, 4 colours, window 2 (generated by analysis.py)

2000 allowed-word sets sampled uniformly from the 2^32 sets, 2 colours, window 5 (numpy default_rng seed 20261031; generated by analysis.py)

5000 allowed-word sets sampled uniformly from the 2^27 sets, 3 colours, window 3 (same seed; generated by analysis.py)

fields.label: Caveats
fields.value:
The claim is a theorem (a non-empty one-dimensional shift of finite type contains a periodic point, from a cycle in its de Bruijn graph); the computation confirms it exhaustively for all two-colour constraints with windows up to 4 and all four-colour constraints with window 2, and by sampling for windows 5 (two colours) and 3 (three colours). The maximal minimal period found (8 for k = 2, w = 4; exactly the two de Bruijn-cycle constraint sets) matches the bound V = k^(w-1).

Satisfiability was operationalised by the existence of a valid word of length 4V + w; by compactness this is equivalent to the existence of a bi-infinite arrangement, but the equivalence itself relies on finiteness of the vertex set, so the two indicators are not logically independent even though they are computed by different algorithms.

Wolfram's 'simple' is read as 'periodic'; the observed minimal periods are small (at most V), but 'simple' is not otherwise quantified.
